```{python}
from panels import show
```

Each table comes from `tests/registry.py`, so every shape here is also a fixture with goldens, and
the gallery and the test suite cannot drift apart. The style is house style's `house_style()`: the
document budget of 41.4em and a scale ceiling of 0.9. Column widths are measured in the face the
tables are set in, `tikz_font`: STIX Two in the house-style PDF, Times everywhere else. Where a
section varies a `HouseStyle` field, the text says which. Every table is numbered in the order the document runs, and headed by its
fixture name and any style changes, so a table can be named by its number.

On the web each table appears twice: the HTML, then the TikZ TeX compiled on its own and converted
to SVG. That image is set in Times at 11pt on a page with no margins, so judge rules, alignment,
spans and wrapping there, and judge width against the margins in the PDF. The PDF shows the TikZ
table in the document's own text block. Render with:

```powershell
$env:QUARTO_PYTHON = "V:\dev\greatest-tables\.venv\Scripts\python.exe"
quarto render guide\gallery.qmd --to house-html   # gallery-house.html
quarto render guide\gallery.qmd --to house-pdf    # gallery-house.pdf, STIX Two
quarto render guide\gallery.qmd --to html         # gallery.html
quarto render guide\gallery.qmd --to pdf          # gallery.pdf, Times
```

## Flat tables

A trivial index is hidden. Text left, numbers right, uniform decimals per column.

```{python}
show('plain')
```

A list of rows with no header row.

```{python}
show('headerless')
```

## Row indexes

Two levels, sparsified: an outer label appears once, at the top of its group, with a rule between
groups.

```{python}
show('row-mi-2')
```

Three levels. Rules at the outer two breaks, none between rows of the innermost level.

```{python}
show('row-mi-3')
```

The same table with `sparsify=False`: every row carries its full label.

```{python}
show('row-mi-3-dense')
```

Four levels, with a year as the innermost level, printed plain because it is tagged `year_cols`.

```{python}
show('row-mi-4')
```

Five levels: the depth at which the rule policy and a fixed depth cap disagree.

```{python}
show('deep-stub')
```

## Horizontal rules

`max_rule_depth` on the three-level index: `'auto'` (the default) rules every break but the
innermost, `0` only the outermost, `1` the outer two, and `None` none at all.

```{python}
show('row-mi-3', max_rule_depth=0)
```

```{python}
show('row-mi-3', max_rule_depth=1)
```

```{python}
show('row-mi-3', max_rule_depth=None)
```

A total row appended to a flat table, set bold with a rule above it.

Subtotals inside the groups of a two-level index, and a grand total, all through `row_flags`.

## Width

The two-prose-column table under three budgets. At 45em it fits by narrowing alone; at 30em it
narrows further; at 24em the prose has reached its minimum, 8em (`min_prose_width_em`), and the
table scales instead of setting the prose a word or two a line.

```{python}
show('wrap-low', max_table_width_em=45)
```

```{python}
show('wrap-low', max_table_width_em=30)
```

```{python}
show('wrap-low', max_table_width_em=24)
```

A table of numbers only has nothing to narrow, so it steps down the scale ladder.

```{python}
show('both-mi', max_table_width_em=24)
```

Twenty number columns against the 41.4em document budget: the ladder stops at 0.6 and the table
still overruns. greater_tables logs that at ERROR, so it shows here, under the cell, even with house
style's logger setting.

```{python}
show('wide-numbers')
```

## Width details

The regressions `dev/check-widths.qmd` used to hold, now fixtures.

A long heading wraps to its widest word, so three narrow columns of numbers sit under wrapped
headings, not three wide columns under one-line headings.

```{python}
show('long-headings')
```

Stub values set at exactly their natural width stay on one line: `Sub 1` and `Sub 2`, not `Sub`
over `1`.

```{python}
show('stub-fits')
```

The em dash, the percent sign, the SI micro and ISO dates are each measured at their true width:
the dashes sit clear of the next column, and the dates leave no trailing gap.

```{python}
show('glyph-widths')
```

A group label wider than the columns beneath it widens the last column it covers instead of
spilling over the rules on either side.

```{python}
show('long-spanner')
```

## Long headings

A long heading over narrow data. The column is as wide as the heading's longest word, so the
heading stacks on as many lines as it needs. Under a budget, the column with the tallest heading
then takes spare width until that heading is no taller than the next tallest; when two tie,
nothing moves.

Four ratio columns under headings of four to seven words.

```{python}
show('long-head-ratios')
```

Y/N flags, one character wide, under headings of three to seven words.

```{python}
show('long-head-flags')
```

Counts of at most three digits.

```{python}
show('long-head-counts')
```

Long leaf headings under column groups.

```{python}
show('long-head-groups')
```

Nine long headings over Y/N and counts: too wide for the budget even with every heading at its
longest word, so the table also scales.

```{python}
show('long-head-many')
```

## Sideways

A table too wide for the text block, set on a page of its own by
`tikz_container_env='sidewaystable'`, with the budget at the text height, 62em. The document needs
`\usepackage{rotating}`. The same Loss Lab shape upright first, scaled to the text width.

```{python}
show('wide-lab')
```

```{python}
show('wide-lab', tikz_container_env='sidewaystable', max_table_width_em=62)
```

Twenty number columns, which overrun the upright budget, sideways.

```{python}
show('wide-numbers', tikz_container_env='sidewaystable', max_table_width_em=62)
```

## Long tables

The first 30 of 250 rows, with the truncation note. A TikZ table is one box and cannot break across
pages, which is why `max_rows` matters in a PDF; the default of 200 rows does not fit a page.

```{python}
show('long')
```

The first 5 of 12.
